Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette: At seventy-five, Kai still measures time by the evening the rape occurred on a quiet Oakland street. The assailant’s complete disregard for bodily autonomy was a profound moral violation that unfolded without warning or recourse. When local police arrived, the encounter offered no safety. An officer’s tone was brisk, his questions laced with skeptical corrections that focused on procedural details rather than Kai’s immediate distress. That specific convergence of boundary-shattering cruelty and authoritative dismissal carved a narrow pathway for what followed. Now, years later, Kai remains hyper-sensitive to any display of public misconduct and the sight of law enforcement, not as abstract concepts, but as immediate physiological alarms. The way the first responder’s posture shifted and the casual dismissal of the initial attack established a pattern Kai’s nervous system never forgot: wrongdoing and official scrutiny always arrived together. In the months that followed, Kai’s attempts to reconstruct the event collapsed into disjointed fragments. There was no coherent story to tell, no clear sequence that could be laid out on paper or spoken aloud without the narrative fracturing. When the mind tried to reach back, only isolated sensory intrusions returned. Kai would suddenly hear the sharp click of a car door or the muffled echo of a voice from the street, the sounds arriving unbidden during routine tasks. Alongside them came the vivid, lingering taste of copper and wet pavement, flooding the mouth whenever the auditory fragments surfaced. Whenever Kai encountered the sight of a uniform or heard someone speak with dismissive authority, the mind immediately reached backward, pulling forth the fragmented recollections of the attack. The inability to construct a coherent narrative of the assault, combined with the sudden intrusion of those metallic tastes and echoing voices, steadily convinced Kai that their ongoing reactions meant they were going crazy. These unbidden sensations did not merely visit; they actively pulled Kai further into a state of paranoid self-doubt. The fragmentation seeped directly into Kai’s professional life at a downtown financial firm. As a financial analyst, Kai spent days reviewing compliance reports and attending quarterly audits, environments where peer review was routine. During a recent budget reconciliation, a senior partner pointed out a discrepancy in Kai’s projections and offered a stern correction. When a compliance auditor criticized a line item on Kai’s spreadsheet, that authoritative criticism bypassed professional logic and directly activated the conviction that they could no longer rely on themselves. Work, once a source of structure, now felt hollow, each spreadsheet blurring into a landscape where nothing held any meaning. Kai began arriving early to avoid elevator rides with colleagues, citing fatigue rather than the sudden dread that accompanied the smell of polished shoes or the sound of a keycard swiping. Over time, the pattern hardened into a daily habit of withdrawal. Because the disjointed memories kept resurfacing without warning, Kai’s attention became permanently locked on environmental cues, turning ordinary workplace interactions into potent triggers for renewed dread. Whenever the metallic taste returned, Kai’s focus snapped toward the office doorway, scanning for uniformed personnel or any sign of inappropriate conduct, which in turn flooded the mind with more fragmented recollections. The loop tightened with exhausting precision: sensory intrusions confirmed the belief that sanity was slipping, and that belief amplified the dread of everyday interactions. At seventy-five, widowed and increasingly isolated, Kai finally scheduled an intake. The hesitation in the waiting room was less about the appointment and more about the terror that speaking the truth would finally shatter the remaining composure. Yet, beneath the fear of going completely unstable, there was a quiet, stubborn hope that someone might help untangle the memories before the meaning of the rest of life vanished entirely.
